title: Static / published page
summary: A published origin with no first-party login or API. Work TLS, browser policy, Host/authority, path serving, leftover files, and client framing — then stop. Auth, CSRF, business logic, and interpreter injection are out of scope unless reconnaissance proves a backend.

groups.title: TLS / transport
groups.summary: Certificate, protocol, cipher, and HTTP-to-HTTPS behaviour on the public host.

checks.title: Check SSL config — testssl
checks.why: Weak protocols, expired or mismatched certificates, or a broken chain on a public host.
checks.validate: A protocol, cipher, or certificate defect is reproduced by testssl or an equivalent client — not a scanner grade alone.

variants.name: Fast testssl scan
variants.payload: testssl.sh --fast --sneaky https://www.example.com
variants.expect: SSLv2/3, TLS 1.0/1.1, export/NULL/RC4/3DES, expired or hostname-mismatched cert, incomplete chain.
variants.why: A quick testssl run inventories protocols, ciphers, and certificate issues in one pass.

variants.name: Protocol and cipher only
variants.payload: testssl.sh -p -E https://www.example.com
variants.expect: Which protocol versions and cipher suites the host actually offers.
variants.why: Restricting the scan to protocols and ciphers isolates the config from noise.

variants.name: Certificate and chain
variants.payload: testssl.sh -S https://www.example.com
variants.expect: SANs, validity window, issuer, and whether intermediates are served.
variants.why: Focusing on the chain surfaces expiry, hostname, and completeness issues.

variants.name: openssl s_client handshake
variants.payload: echo | openssl s_client -connect www.example.com:443 -servername www.example.com -tls1_0 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -dates -subject -ext subjectAltName
variants.expect: TLS 1.0 handshake succeeds (bad) or is refused (good). Repeat with -tls1_1 and -tls1_2.
variants.why: A manual handshake confirms a single protocol or certificate fact without a scanner.

checks.title: HTTP → HTTPS redirect
checks.why: Plain HTTP still serves content, cookies, or a redirect to the wrong host.
checks.validate: The first HTTP response is a redirect to the canonical HTTPS host and carries no Set-Cookie or body secrets.

variants.name: Plain GET on port 80
variants.payload:
GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Connection: close
variants.expect: 301/308 to https://www.example.com/… No body, no Set-Cookie.
variants.why: The plaintext response decides whether HTTP is a downgrade path.

variants.name: HTTP with a path and query
variants.payload:
GET /docs/index.html?ref=nav HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Connection: close
variants.expect: Redirect preserves a safe path and drops tokens if any were present.
variants.why: A path+query over HTTP checks the redirect preserves the full request.

variants.name: HTTP Host mismatch
variants.payload:
GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: evil.example
Connection: close
variants.expect: Reject or redirect to the canonical HTTPS host — never to https://evil.example/.
variants.why: A mismatched Host over HTTP can yield a redirect to a different vhost.

checks.title: Deprecated TLS versions
checks.why: SSLv2/3 and TLS 1.0/1.1 still offered on the public host.
checks.validate: A real client completes a handshake on a deprecated protocol. A scanner grade alone is not a finding.

variants.name: TLS 1.0 handshake
variants.payload: echo | openssl s_client -connect www.example.com:443 -servername www.example.com -tls1 2>/dev/null | head -n 20
variants.expect: Handshake refused (good) or completed (reportable if a browser or library can still negotiate it).
variants.why: A successful TLS 1.0 handshake is the deprecated-protocol finding.

variants.name: TLS 1.1 handshake
variants.payload: echo | openssl s_client -connect www.example.com:443 -servername www.example.com -tls1_1 2>/dev/null | head -n 20
variants.expect: Same as TLS 1.0. Repeat with -tls1_2 and -tls1_3 as the control.
observe: ALPN / cipher on the deprecated handshake
variants.why: TLS 1.1 is likewise deprecated and must be refused.

checks.title: Weak cipher suites
checks.why: NULL, export, RC4, 3DES, or anonymous DH suites are still offered.
checks.validate: testssl or openssl lists a weak suite that a client can actually negotiate — not a historic cipher in documentation.

variants.name: Cipher inventory
variants.payload: testssl.sh -E https://www.example.com
variants.expect: No NULL/EXPORT/RC4/3DES/anon. Prefer AEAD (AES-GCM / CHACHA20-POLY1305).
observe: Whether a weak suite is selectable
variants.why: Listing suites shows whether weak ciphers are offered.

variants.name: Force a weak suite
variants.payload: echo | openssl s_client -connect www.example.com:443 -servername www.example.com -cipher "RC4-SHA:DES-CBC3-SHA:NULL" 2>/dev/null | head -n 15
variants.expect: Handshake must fail. Success is the finding.
variants.why: Negotiating a weak suite proves it is actually usable, not just listed.

checks.title: Certificate configuration
checks.why: Expired, hostname-mismatched, incomplete-chain, or wrong-SAN certificates break trust or enable look-alike hosts.
checks.validate: A real client rejects the chain, or a SAN does not cover the host users type. Do not report a missing CT log as a finding.

variants.name: Names and dates
variants.payload: echo | openssl s_client -connect www.example.com:443 -servername www.example.com 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -dates -subject -issuer -ext subjectAltName
variants.expect: NotBefore/NotAfter cover now. SAN includes www and the apex if users hit both.
variants.why: Hostname and validity are the two certificate facts that matter to a visitor.

variants.name: Chain completeness
variants.payload: testssl.sh -S https://www.example.com
variants.expect: Intermediates are served. A leaf-only chain that still works via AIA is a lead, not always a finding.
variants.why: An incomplete chain breaks trust even when the leaf is valid.

checks.title: Mixed content
checks.why: An HTTPS page still loads scripts, styles, or form actions over http://.
checks.validate: A script, stylesheet, or form target is fetched or submitted over HTTP on the live page. An http:// in a comment is not a finding.

variants.name: Active mixed content
variants.payload:
View-source and DevTools Network on https://www.example.com/
Grep: src="http://  href="http://  action="http://  url(http://
variants.expect: Any script/style/iframe/form over HTTP on an HTTPS page. Images are passive mixed content — lower impact.
observe: http:// requests on an https document
variants.why: Active mixed content (script/iframe) is blocked by modern browsers but still a risk on old ones.

variants.name: Upgrade-Insecure-Requests
variants.payload:
GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Connection: close
variants.expect: Content-Security-Policy: upgrade-insecure-requests is a control, not a substitute for fixing the URLs.
observe: Whether http:// URLs remain in markup
variants.why: The upgrade directive reveals whether the origin intends to move off http://.

groups.title: Security headers
groups.summary: HSTS, CSP, framing, nosniff, referrer, and the missing-header baseline.

checks.title: Missing security headers
checks.why: A scanner lead is not a finding. Map each absent or weak header to a real browser exposure on this page.
checks.validate: Each reported gap is tied to a page that actually needs that policy, or is recorded as informational with no impact.

variants.name: Capture the live header set
variants.payload:
GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Connection: close
variants.expect: Record Strict-Transport-Security, Content-Security-Policy, X-Frame-Options, X-Content-Type-Options, Referrer-Policy, Permissions-Policy, Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy, Cache-Control.
variants.why: The actual header set is the ground truth before any header judgement.

variants.name: HTML vs asset vs error
variants.payload:
GET /this-path-should-404 HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Connection: close
variants.expect: Error and static-asset responses often drop policies that the homepage has. Compare / , /404, and a .js / .css URL.
variants.why: Different response classes often drop headers the homepage has.

variants.name: curl header dump
variants.payload: curl -sI https://www.example.com/
variants.expect: Same set as Repeater. A missing header is a lead — impact is proven on the specific check below.
variants.why: A single curl -I confirms headers across paths without a browser.

checks.title: Check HSTS enforcement
checks.why: Without HSTS a network attacker can keep the victim on HTTP or strip the upgrade.
checks.validate: HTTPS responses on the real host send a long-lived HSTS policy, and HTTP does not serve the page.

variants.name: Read the HSTS policy
variants.payload:
GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Connection: close
variants.expect: Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains (preload optional). max-age under 6 months is weak.
variants.why: The HSTS max-age and includeSubDomains are read directly.

variants.name: HSTS must not appear on HTTP
variants.payload:
GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Connection: close
variants.expect: An HSTS header on a plaintext response is ignored by browsers. Confirm it is only set on HTTPS.
variants.why: HSTS on plaintext is ignored and signals a misconfiguration.

variants.name: Apex vs www
variants.payload:
GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com
Connection: close
variants.expect: If users hit the apex, that host needs its own HSTS (or includeSubDomains from a parent that they actually visit first).
variants.why: HSTS is host-specific, so the apex and www can diverge.

variants.name: preload readiness (informational)
variants.payload: Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains; preload
variants.expect: Do not report missing preload. Report missing or short max-age, or HTTP still serving content.
variants.why: Preload eligibility is informational; the real control is the header itself.

checks.title: Check CSP
checks.why: A missing, report-only, or unsafe-inline CSP does not stop script the page already loads — but it is the impact-reduction control for XSS and unexpected script sources.
checks.validate: The enforced policy (not Report-Only) would block a script source the application does not intend. A missing CSP on a static brochure is informational unless a script sink exists.

variants.name: Read the enforced policy
variants.payload:
GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Connection: close
variants.expect: Content-Security-Policy (enforced) vs Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only. Report-Only is not protection.
observe: Missing directives that matter on this page
variants.why: Report-Only is not protection — the enforced policy is what a real browser applies.

variants.name: unsafe-inline / unsafe-eval / wildcards
variants.payload: Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; script-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline' 'unsafe-eval' https: data: *
variants.expect: script-src with 'unsafe-inline', 'unsafe-eval', data:, https:, or * does not constrain script. object-src should be 'none'.
observe: Missing directives that matter on this page
variants.why: These sources defeat CSP’s purpose, so reading them directly is the fast check.

variants.name: Nonce or hash without unsafe fallback
variants.payload: Content-Security-Policy: script-src 'nonce-r4nd0m' 'unsafe-inline'
variants.expect: A nonce plus 'unsafe-inline' makes the nonce useless in supporting browsers. Hashes plus 'unsafe-inline' have the same problem.
observe: Missing directives that matter on this page
variants.why: unsafe-inline alongside a nonce/hash silently nullifies the nonce/hash in supporting browsers.

variants.name: base-uri and form-action
variants.payload: Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; base-uri 'self'; form-action 'self'; object-src 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none'
variants.expect: Missing base-uri allows <base href> to retarget relative URLs. Missing form-action allows form exfiltration.
observe: Missing directives that matter on this page
variants.why: base-uri and form-action limit DOM and form-exfiltration even when script-src is locked down.

variants.name: Duplicate or conflicting CSP
variants.payload:
GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Connection: close
variants.expect: Two Content-Security-Policy headers combine as an AND in modern browsers, but a CDN and origin can silently weaken each other. Record both raw values.
observe: Missing directives that matter on this page
variants.why: Two policies AND together in modern browsers, but a CDN and origin can silently weaken each other.

checks.title: Clickjacking check
checks.why: A third-party page can frame this origin and overlay or steal clicks if neither CSP frame-ancestors nor X-Frame-Options forbids it.
checks.validate: A cross-origin iframe of the real page either fails to load or the page has no sensitive control. A missing header on a brochure with no UI is informational.

variants.name: Read framing headers
variants.payload:
GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Connection: close
variants.expect: Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'none' (or an explicit allowlist). X-Frame-Options: DENY or SAMEORIGIN must not contradict CSP.
variants.why: frame-ancestors and X-Frame-Options decide whether the page can be framed.

variants.name: Cross-origin iframe
variants.payload:
<!doctype html>
<title>frame test</title>
<iframe src="https://www.example.com/" style="width:100%;height:100%"></iframe>
variants.expect: The iframe stays blank / errors when frame-ancestors or XFO is set. If the page renders, framing is allowed.
variants.why: An actual frame load confirms or refutes the header reading.

variants.name: sandbox + allow-from leftovers
variants.payload: <iframe src="https://www.example.com/" sandbox="allow-scripts allow-forms"></iframe>
variants.expect: X-Frame-Options: ALLOW-FROM is obsolete and ignored. sandbox on the attacker iframe is not a server defense.
variants.why: Legacy sandbox/allow-from attributes are ignored by modern browsers and can confuse the policy.

variants.name: XFO vs frame-ancestors conflict
variants.payload:
X-Frame-Options: DENY
Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors https://partner.example
variants.expect: CSP wins in modern browsers. Record which policy a real browser applied, not which header a scanner listed.
variants.why: CSP frame-ancestors and X-Frame-Options can contradict each other.

checks.title: nosniff, Referrer-Policy, Cache-Control
checks.why: User-controlled or downloadable files can be sniffed as HTML; referrers can leak tokens; HTML can be stored in a shared cache.
checks.validate: A realistic load context shows sniffing, referrer leakage, or shared-cache reuse — not just a missing header name.

variants.name: X-Content-Type-Options
variants.payload:
GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Connection: close
variants.expect: X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff on HTML and on any user-influenced or downloadable body.
variants.why: nosniff stops MIME-sniffing user-influenced bodies into HTML.

variants.name: Referrer-Policy
variants.payload: Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin
variants.expect: If any URL on this origin ever carries a token or internal path, a missing or unsafe-url policy leaks it cross-origin.
variants.why: Referrer-Policy bounds what the URL leaks cross-origin.

variants.name: Cache-Control on HTML
variants.payload:
GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Connection: close
variants.expect: Public marketing HTML may be cacheable. Authenticated or personalized HTML must be private / no-store.
variants.why: Cache-Control decides whether a shared cache can store the page.

checks.title: X-Content-Type-Options
checks.why: User-influenced or downloadable bodies can be sniffed as HTML without nosniff.
checks.validate: A realistic content-type mismatch is executed as HTML, or a downloadable user file is sniffed. Missing nosniff on a brochure is informational.

variants.name: Read nosniff
variants.payload:
GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Connection: close
variants.expect: X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff on HTML and on any user-influenced or downloadable body.
observe: Header present on a .js / download URL
variants.why: The nosniff flag on user-influenced bodies is the control.

variants.name: HTML vs download
variants.payload:
GET /assets/app.js HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Connection: close
variants.expect: Assets and error pages often drop nosniff. Compare / , a .js, and a 404.
variants.why: Downloadable and error responses often drop nosniff that the homepage sets.

checks.title: Referrer Policy
checks.why: Tokens or internal paths in the URL leak cross-origin via Referer.
checks.validate: A cross-origin navigation from a token-bearing URL actually sends the secret. Missing Referrer-Policy on a brochure with no secrets is informational.

variants.name: Read the policy
variants.payload:
GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Connection: close
variants.expect: Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin or stricter. unsafe-url is the weak case.
observe: Whether any URL on this origin carries a token
variants.why: The policy value is read before judging leak risk.

variants.name: Meta vs header
variants.payload: <meta name="referrer" content="no-referrer">
variants.expect: A meta referrer can override or conflict with the header. Record which one a browser applied.
observe: Actual Referer on a cross-origin click
variants.why: A meta referrer-policy and the header can disagree; the effective one wins.

checks.title: Permissions Policy
checks.why: Camera, geolocation, payment, and similar powerful features stay available to this origin or its iframes.
checks.validate: A powerful feature that this page does not need can be invoked, or an embedded frame inherits it. Absence on a static brochure is informational.

variants.name: Read Permissions-Policy
variants.payload:
GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Connection: close
variants.expect: Permissions-Policy (or Feature-Policy leftover). camera=(), geolocation=(), microphone=(), payment=() for pages that do not use them.
variants.why: Permissions-Policy restricts powerful features per-origin/per-frame.

variants.name: Feature-Policy leftover
variants.payload: Feature-Policy: camera 'none'; geolocation 'none'
variants.expect: Feature-Policy is obsolete. Browsers honour Permissions-Policy. Do not report a missing Feature-Policy.
variants.why: The deprecated Feature-Policy header is ignored by modern browsers.

checks.title: Cross-Origin Resource Policy
checks.why: Sensitive responses can be included cross-origin as no-cors resources without CORP.
checks.validate: A cross-origin no-cors read of a non-public body is possible. CORP missing on public marketing HTML is informational.

variants.name: Read CORP
variants.payload:
GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Connection: close
variants.expect: Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy: same-origin or same-site on responses that must not be embedded cross-origin.
variants.why: CORP controls whether a response can be embedded as a no-cors resource.

variants.name: no-cors embed
variants.payload: <script>fetch("https://www.example.com/private.json", {mode:"no-cors"})</script>
variants.expect: Opaque success is not a finding. A readable non-public body is. Public HTML does not need CORP.
variants.why: An actual no-cors fetch/embed confirms whether the policy is enforced.

checks.title: Cache-Control
checks.why: Personalized or authenticated HTML stored in a shared cache is served to the next user.
checks.validate: A shared cache or another browser session receives a personalized body. Public marketing HTML may be cacheable.

variants.name: Read caching headers
variants.payload:
GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Connection: close
variants.expect: Cache-Control, Pragma, Expires, Vary. Authenticated or personalized HTML must be private / no-store.
variants.why: Cache-Control on HTML is the shared-cache control.

variants.name: Shared vs private
variants.payload: Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000
variants.expect: Fine on hashed static assets. A finding on HTML that differs per user or carries a session.
observe: CDN cache hit on a second client
variants.why: A private/personalised body served with public caching is the shared-cache leak.

groups.title: Host / authority
groups.summary: Host header injection, forwarding headers, and absolute-form request targets.

checks.title: Host Header Injection
checks.why: The edge or origin uses Host (or a forwarding header) to pick a vhost, build absolute URLs, or key a cache.
checks.validate: The injected authority appears in a Location, generated link, cache key, or a different virtual host — not only in an error page echo.

variants.name: Arbitrary Host
variants.payload:
GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: evil.example
Connection: close
variants.expect: 400/421/404, or the canonical site ignoring Host. Vulnerable if Location, asset URLs, or a password/reset-style link use evil.example.
variants.why: The most basic probe: does the origin trust an attacker-chosen Host for routing, generated URLs, or cache keys?

variants.name: Duplicate Host
variants.payload:
GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Host: evil.example
Connection: close
variants.expect: Which Host is processed? Redirect, routing, or cache disagreement between hops is the finding — not a 200 alone.
variants.why: Tests front-end/back-end disagreement in Host parsing.

variants.name: Duplicate Host reversed
variants.payload:
GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: evil.example
Host: www.example.com
Connection: close
variants.expect: Compare with the previous order. Front-end and origin must agree on first vs last Host.
variants.why: Order sensitivity: some stacks take the first Host, others the last.

variants.name: Host normalization
variants.payload:
GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: EXAMPLE.COM
Connection: close
variants.expect: Also try example.com. and example.com:443. Case, trailing dot, and default port must not change routing or generated URLs.
variants.why: Case, trailing dot, and default port must not change routing or generated URLs.

variants.name: Host with port
variants.payload:
GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com:443
Connection: close
variants.expect: Treated as the same host. Vulnerable if generated URLs become https://www.example.com:443@evil.example/ or similar parse tricks.
variants.why: A port-suffixed Host must resolve to the same authority, not a parse trick.

variants.name: Absolute-form request target
variants.payload:
GET https://evil.example/ HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Connection: close
variants.expect: Origin-form only, or the absolute URL is ignored. Vulnerable if routing or generated links follow evil.example.
variants.why: Absolute-form request-target lets a request carry a second authority alongside Host.

variants.name: X-Forwarded-Host
variants.payload:
GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
X-Forwarded-Host: evil.example
Connection: close
variants.expect: Ignored unless the hop is a trusted proxy that overwrites the value. Vulnerable if Location or links use evil.example.
variants.why: Tests whether a trusted proxy header overrides the externally controlled authority.

variants.name: X-Host / X-Forwarded-Server
variants.payload:
GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
X-Host: evil.example
X-Forwarded-Server: evil.example
Connection: close
variants.expect: Same as X-Forwarded-Host. Some Java and IIS stacks prefer these over Host.
variants.why: Java/IIS stacks sometimes prefer these over X-Forwarded-Host.

variants.name: Forwarded (RFC 7239)
variants.payload:
GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Forwarded: host=evil.example;proto=https
Connection: close
variants.expect: Ignored unless the edge authenticates the hop. Vulnerable if proto or host is trusted for redirects or cookies.
variants.why: The standardised Forwarded header must only be trusted from an authenticated hop.

variants.name: X-Forwarded-Proto downgrade
variants.payload:
GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
X-Forwarded-Proto: http
X-Forwarded-Scheme: http
Connection: close
variants.expect: Canonical https links stay https. Vulnerable if the app emits http://… cookies or redirects.
variants.why: A downgrade to http:// must not flip cookies or redirects to plaintext.

variants.name: Line-wrapped / padded Host
variants.payload:
GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Host: www.example.com.evil.example
Connection: close
variants.expect: Suffix and look-alike hosts must not match a substring allowlist (example.com inside attacker.example.com.evil.example).
variants.why: Suffix and look-alike hosts probe substring allowlist bypasses.

checks.title: Absolute URL injection
checks.why: A path, parameter, or generated link accepts an absolute or protocol-relative URL and navigates or loads off-origin.
checks.validate: The browser or a Location header ends on an origin you control. Reflected text without navigation is not enough.

variants.name: Absolute HTTPS
variants.payload:
GET /?next=https://evil.example/ HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Connection: close
variants.expect: No 3xx to evil.example. Repeat for next, url, redirect, return, dest, continue, redir, target.
variants.why: An absolute HTTPS destination tests the open-redirect boundary.

variants.name: Protocol-relative
variants.payload:
GET /?next=//evil.example/ HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Connection: close
variants.expect: Rejected or treated as a relative path. Vulnerable if Location becomes //evil.example/.
variants.why: A //-relative URL is coerced to the page's scheme, widening the redirect.

variants.name: Backslash and encoded slash
variants.payload:
GET /?next=/\evil.example/ HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Connection: close
variants.expect: Some parsers treat /\evil.example as a scheme-relative URL. Also try /%2f%2fevil.example/ and /%5cevil.example/.
variants.why: Backslash and encoded-slash variants defeat naive URL parsers.

variants.name: javascript: and data:
variants.payload:
GET /?next=javascript:alert(1) HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Connection: close
variants.expect: Must not become a navigable Location or an href. data:text/html,… is the same class.
variants.why: A javascript: or data: URL in a navigation sink is a DOM-XSS vector.

variants.name: Open-redirect in static HTML
variants.payload: continue
variants.expect: Grep published HTML and JS for // , https://, location.href, window.open, and meta refresh built from query or hash.
variants.why: A client-side redirect in static HTML is an open redirect with no server involvement.

checks.title: HTTP method handling
checks.why: TRACE, PUT, DELETE, or method override changes behaviour the page did not intend.
checks.validate: An unexpected method returns a body, echoes input (TRACE), or changes state. OPTIONS listing a method is a lead, not a finding.

variants.name: OPTIONS
variants.payload:
OPTIONS / HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Connection: close
variants.expect: Allow / Access-Control-Allow-Methods. TRACE, PUT, DELETE on a static origin should not be live.
variants.why: OPTIONS discloses the allowed methods a route claims.

variants.name: TRACE
variants.payload:
TRACE / HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
X-WAPT: probe
Connection: close
variants.expect: TRACE must not echo headers (XST). 405/501 is the secure case.
observe: Whether X-WAPT is reflected in the body
variants.why: A live TRACE is an XST vector against HttpOnly cookies.

variants.name: PUT / DELETE
variants.payload:
PUT /wapt-method-probe.txt HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Content-Type: text/plain
Content-Length: 4
Connection: close

wapt
variants.expect: Must not store a file. Follow with GET of the same path. Stop after one confirmed write and delete the object.
variants.why: An enabled PUT/DELETE on a static origin can overwrite or remove content.

checks.title: Open redirect
checks.why: A parameter or generated link accepts an absolute or protocol-relative URL and navigates off-origin.
checks.validate: The browser or a Location header ends on an origin you control. Reflected text without navigation is not enough.

variants.name: Absolute HTTPS
variants.payload:
GET /?next=https://evil.example/ HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Connection: close
variants.expect: No 3xx to evil.example. Repeat for next, url, redirect, return, dest, continue, redir, target.
variants.why: An absolute HTTPS destination tests the open-redirect boundary.

variants.name: Protocol-relative
variants.payload:
GET /?next=//evil.example/ HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Connection: close
variants.expect: Rejected or treated as a relative path. Vulnerable if Location becomes //evil.example/.
observe: Whether the path is treated as relative
variants.why: A //-relative URL is coerced to the page's scheme.

variants.name: Backslash parse
variants.payload:
GET /?next=/\evil.example/ HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Connection: close
variants.expect: Some parsers treat /\evil.example as scheme-relative. Also try /%2f%2fevil.example/.
variants.why: Backslash handling differs between the filter and the browser.

checks.title: HTTP request smuggling
checks.why: Front-end and origin disagree on Content-Length vs Transfer-Encoding, so a second request can be prepended.
checks.validate: A desync is demonstrated with a harmless marker on an authorized target, then stopped. Do not desync production traffic. Mapping hops first is mandatory.

variants.name: Map the hops first
variants.payload: Record CDN / proxy / origin. Confirm a maintenance window. One paired probe at a time. Stop on queue anomalies.
variants.expect: Do not spray. WAPT-SMUG-001 is the prerequisite. This check is Confirm until hops are known.
variants.why: Identifying the CDN/proxy/origin chain is the prerequisite for any desync probe.

variants.name: CL.TE probe shape (authorized lab only)
variants.payload:
POST / HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Content-Length: 6
Transfer-Encoding: chunked
Connection: close

0

X
variants.expect: A 400/timeout/desynced next response is a lead. Confirm with a single follow-up GET for a marker you placed. Never poison shared-user traffic.
variants.why: A CL.TE differential is only ever run in an isolated, authorised window.

checks.title: HTTP method override
checks.why: X-HTTP-Method-Override, X-Method-Override, or _method lets a request change its effective verb, which can bypass verb-based access control.
checks.validate: An override that reaches a verb the app would otherwise deny (e.g. DELETE on a read-only endpoint) is the finding.

variants.name: X-HTTP-Method-Override
variants.payload:
GET /api/v1/resource/1001 HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
X-HTTP-Method-Override: DELETE
Connection: close
variants.expect: If the app honours the override, the effective verb changes — compare status/behaviour vs plain GET.
variants.why: Proxies and frameworks that trust the header re-route the verb, so a GET can become a destructive call.

variants.name: _method body field
variants.payload:
POST /api/v1/resource/1001 HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
Content-Length: 15

_method=DELETE
variants.expect: Some stacks read _method from the body. Compare against the actual POST behaviour.
variants.why: Form-parsing frameworks read the verb from the body, so the header-based fix may miss it.

groups.title: Paths and files
groups.summary: Directory enumeration, listing, traversal, leftovers, and well-known files.

checks.title: Directory enumeration
checks.why: Predictable paths expose admin panels, backups, source, or environment files on a published origin.
checks.validate: A path returns non-public content (config, source, backup, listing, or an unexpected application). A 403 on /admin is a lead, not a finding.

variants.name: robots, sitemap, security.txt
variants.payload:
GET /robots.txt HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Connection: close
variants.expect: Disallow entries and sitemap URLs are leads. Also fetch /sitemap.xml and /.well-known/security.txt.
variants.why: These publisher-authored files seed the route inventory before any brute force.

variants.name: Common published leftovers
variants.payload:
/.git/HEAD
/.svn/entries
/.env
/.env.local
/.env.production
/web.config
/WP-config.php.bak
/backup.zip
/backup.tar.gz
/site.zip
/www.zip
/dump.sql
/composer.json
/package.json
/server-status
/server-info
/.DS_Store
/Thumbs.db
/crossdomain.xml
/clientaccesspolicy.xml
variants.expect: Any 200 with real content is in-scope disclosure. Confirm the body, do not assume from status alone.
variants.why: Common leftover names surface backups and admin paths.

variants.name: Hidden and leftover indexes
variants.payload:
/admin/
/administrator/
/login/
/dashboard/
/staging/
/dev/
/test/
/old/
/backup/
/bak/
/tmp/
/private/
/internal/
/.well-known/openid-configuration
/.well-known/change-password
variants.expect: A different application, default page, or auth wall that the scope document did not mention.
variants.why: Hidden indexes and leftover paths are leads, not findings, until confirmed.

variants.name: ffuf wordlist (authorized, low rate)
variants.payload: ffuf -u https://www.example.com/FUZZ -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/common.txt -mc 200,204,301,302,307,401,403 -rate 20 -t 2
variants.expect: Keep rate low. Follow interesting hits by hand. A 403 is not a finding.
variants.why: A low-rate ffuf run widens discovery only when the client authorises it.

variants.name: Burp Content Discovery
variants.payload: Burp Suite → Target → Site map → right-click the in-scope host → Engagement tools → Discover content. Start from /, keep recursion shallow, and review interesting 200/301/302/401/403 responses by hand.
variants.expect: New routes, backup extensions, or unlinked files. A discovered path is a lead; validate the response body before reporting.
variants.why: Burp Content Discovery reuses the live session and proxy scope, making it the quickest authenticated discovery pass.

variants.name: Gobuster directory pass
variants.payload: gobuster dir -u https://www.example.com/ -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/common.txt -x bak,old,zip,tar.gz,conf,json,xml -s 200,204,301,302,307,401,403 -t 2
variants.expect: Review status, redirect target, content type, and response size. Keep concurrency within the agreed rate.
variants.why: Gobuster provides a second discovery implementation and an explicit extension pass for deployment leftovers.

variants.name: Filter soft 404s and uniform responses
variants.payload: ffuf -u https://www.example.com/FUZZ -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/common.txt -ac -fc 404 -rate 20 -t 2
variants.expect: Use -ac first, then filter stable false-positive sizes with -fs <length>. Compare 200, 301, 302, and 403 bodies instead of trusting status alone.
variants.why: Automatic calibration and response-size filtering stop a custom 200 soft-404 page from flooding the result set.

variants.name: Bounded recursive discovery
variants.payload: ffuf -u https://www.example.com/FUZZ -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/common.txt -recursion -recursion-depth 2 -rate 15 -t 2
variants.expect: Recurse only into confirmed directories. Stop on unstable latency, rate limiting, or a growing result tree outside the agreed scope.
variants.why: A shallow recursive pass finds nested admin, archive, and framework paths without an unbounded crawl.

checks.title: Directory listing
checks.why: An index-less directory prints names of backups, source maps, or objects that were never linked.
checks.validate: The response body is an autoindex (Index of /…, S3 listing, or equivalent) and names objects that should not be public.

variants.name: Trailing-slash directory
variants.payload:
GET /assets/ HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Connection: close
variants.expect: Index of /assets, or an S3/GCS XML listing. Repeat for /static/, /uploads/, /images/, /css/, /js/, /backup/.
variants.why: An index-less directory with a trailing slash prints its file names.

variants.name: Parent of a known file
variants.payload:
GET /css/ HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Connection: close
variants.expect: If /css/app.css exists, /css/ often lists maps, .bak, and old hashes.
variants.why: Walking to the parent of a known file can expose sibling assets.

variants.name: Object-storage listing
variants.payload:
GET /?prefix=&delimiter=/ HTTP/1.1
Host: files.example.com
Connection: close
variants.expect: S3-style ListBucketResult XML. Also try ?list-type=2 on the bucket hostname.
variants.why: An S3/GCS-style listing probe checks for public object enumeration.

checks.title: Path traversal
checks.why: The file server joins a user-influenced path onto a document root and does not canonicalize before read.
checks.validate: A traversal reads a file outside the intended directory. On production use a canary you placed, not /etc/passwd.

variants.name: Dot-dot slash
variants.payload:
GET /assets/../../../wapt-canary.txt HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Connection: close
variants.expect: The canary (or a known file above the alias) is returned. Stop after one confirmed read.
observe: Body is the canary / outside the alias?
variants.why: The canonical ../ escape; the canary file makes a positive read unambiguous.

variants.name: URL-encoded separators
variants.payload:
GET /assets/..%2f..%2f..%2fwapt-canary.txt HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Connection: close
variants.expect: Same as ../ after one decode. Also try %2e%2e/ and %2e%2e%2f.
observe: Body is the canary / outside the alias?
variants.why: An edge may decode %2f before the path check, letting the origin see a traversal the edge did not.

variants.name: Double-encoded
variants.payload:
GET /assets/..%252f..%252f..%252fwapt-canary.txt HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Connection: close
variants.expect: Edge decodes once, origin decodes again. Vulnerable if the second decode is after the path check.
observe: Body is the canary / outside the alias?
variants.why: Two decode layers (edge then origin) can resurrect a traversal after the first check.

variants.name: Nested-dot and backslash
variants.payload:
GET /assets/....//....//wapt-canary.txt HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Connection: close
variants.expect: Also try ..\..\wapt-canary.txt and /assets/..%5c..%5cwapt-canary.txt on IIS/Windows origins.
observe: Body is the canary / outside the alias?
variants.why: Windows/IIS collapse backslashes and nested dots differently than Unix path parsers.

variants.name: Null byte and semicolon (legacy)
variants.payload:
GET /assets/..%00/../wapt-canary.txt HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Connection: close
variants.expect: Rare on modern stacks. Also /assets/wapt-canary.txt%00.css and /assets/wapt-canary.txt;.css.
observe: Body is the canary / outside the alias?
variants.why: Legacy stacks truncate at %00 or treat ; as a path separator — rare but still worth one probe.

variants.name: Alias / off-by-slash
variants.payload:
GET /static../wapt-canary.txt HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Connection: close
variants.expect: nginx alias /static without a trailing slash can treat /static../ as outside the prefix. Also try /static../ and /static/../.
observe: Body is the canary / outside the alias?
variants.why: An nginx alias without a trailing slash can serve outside the intended prefix.

checks.title: Backups, VCS, and env files
checks.why: Editor swap files, old deploys, .git, and .env are the highest-value static-site findings.
checks.validate: The retrieved file contains source, credentials, or a complete tree — not an empty 200 or a generic error page.

variants.name: Git metadata
variants.payload:
GET /.git/HEAD HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Connection: close
variants.expect: ref: refs/heads/… confirms a repo. Do not mass-extract. Record HEAD, config, and that objects are reachable.
variants.why: .git/HEAD and the objects tree let an attacker reconstruct source.

variants.name: Environment file
variants.payload:
GET /.env HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Connection: close
variants.expect: KEY=value content. Also /.env.local, /.env.production, /config.json, /appsettings.json. Redact secrets in evidence.
variants.why: .env exposes secrets if served.

variants.name: Editor and deploy leftovers
variants.payload:
/index.html.bak
/index.html~
/index.html.old
/index.html.save
/index.php.bak
/app.js.map
/main.js.map
/dist.zip
/release.tar.gz
/web.config.bak
variants.expect: Pair each live file with .bak / ~ / .old / .map. A source map of first-party JS is a lead; secrets inside it are the finding.
variants.why: Swap files, ~-files, and old deploys sit next to live objects.

checks.title: Sensitive file exposure
checks.why: Environment, config, or debug endpoints are published on the origin.
checks.validate: The retrieved file contains secrets or internals — not an empty 200 or a generic error page.

variants.name: Environment file
variants.payload:
GET /.env HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Connection: close
variants.expect: KEY=value content. Also /.env.local, /.env.production, /config.json, /appsettings.json. Redact secrets in evidence.
variants.why: .env is the highest-value static-site secret exposure.

variants.name: Debug and health
variants.payload:
/server-status
/server-info
/phpinfo.php
/actuator
/metrics
/debug
/__debug__
variants.expect: A debug page or metrics with internals is in-scope. A public health 200 with no secrets is informational.
variants.why: Debug/health endpoints publish internal state.

checks.title: Backup file exposure
checks.why: Editor swap files, old deploys, and archives sit next to live objects.
checks.validate: The retrieved file is a real backup or source tree, not an empty 200.

variants.name: Paired leftovers
variants.payload:
/index.html.bak
/index.html~
/index.html.old
/index.html.save
/app.js.bak
/dist.zip
/release.tar.gz
/backup.zip
/www.zip
/dump.sql
variants.expect: Pair each live file with .bak / ~ / .old / archives.
variants.why: A .bak next to a live object is the paired-leftover lead.

variants.name: Archive download
variants.payload:
GET /backup.zip HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Connection: close
variants.expect: A 200 with a zip/tar body is the finding if it contains source or data. Confirm Content-Type and magic bytes.
observe: Whether to stop after one confirmed archive
variants.why: A downloadable archive can bundle source and config.

checks.title: .git exposure
checks.why: A published .git tree lets an attacker reconstruct source and history.
checks.validate: HEAD confirms a repo and objects are reachable. Do not mass-extract. Record HEAD and that config/objects respond.

variants.name: HEAD
variants.payload:
GET /.git/HEAD HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Connection: close
variants.expect: ref: refs/heads/… confirms a repo. Follow with /.git/config — redact remotes if they contain tokens.
variants.why: .git/HEAD is the cheapest positive test for a published tree.

variants.name: Directory vs forbidden
variants.payload:
GET /.git/ HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Connection: close
variants.expect: A listing is extra impact. A 403 on / .git/ with 200 on HEAD is still a finding if objects are reachable.
variants.why: A 403 on /.git/ vs a 200 on /.git/HEAD distinguishes partial exposure.

checks.title: Source map exposure
checks.why: Published maps reconstruct original source and sometimes embed secrets.
checks.validate: A live secret, internal URL, or non-public source tree is in the map. Readable client code alone is not a finding.

variants.name: Direct map URL
variants.payload:
GET /assets/app.js.map HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Connection: close
variants.expect: JSON source map with sourcesContent. Grep for secrets and internal hosts.
variants.why: A direct .map URL reconstructs the original source.

variants.name: sourceMappingURL comment
variants.payload: //# sourceMappingURL=app.js.map
variants.expect: Follow every sourceMappingURL in published JS, including absolute CDN URLs.
variants.why: The trailing sourceMappingURL comment names the map even when it is not linked.

checks.title: Cloud storage exposure
checks.why: A public bucket, listing, or world-readable object sits behind a static origin or a sibling hostname.
checks.validate: An object you should not read is retrieved, or a listing names private keys. Do not write to the bucket.

variants.name: Guess the bucket host
variants.payload:
files.example.com
cdn.example.com
static.example.com
example-prod.s3.amazonaws.com
storage.googleapis.com/example
variants.expect: Inventory from JS, DNS, and certificate SANs. Confirm with a GET of a known public object first.
variants.why: The bucket host is derived from the origin naming pattern.

variants.name: Listing probe
variants.payload:
GET /?list-type=2 HTTP/1.1
Host: files.example.com
Connection: close
variants.expect: S3 ListBucketResult or GCS XML. Also try ?prefix=&delimiter=/. A listing of private keys is the finding.
variants.why: A listing/prefix probe checks for public object enumeration.

checks.title: robots.txt review
checks.why: robots.txt reveals hidden paths, admin prefixes, and internal hostnames the publisher did not want indexed.
checks.validate: A robots.txt entry is a lead, never a finding — map each Disallow to the route inventory and confirm the path exists before reporting disclosure.

variants.name: Read robots.txt
variants.payload:
GET /robots.txt HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Connection: close
variants.expect: Disallow entries are leads; cross-reference against DNS and the sitemap to build the route inventory.
variants.why: An index-blocking directive is metadata, not a control — it tells you which paths are worth confirming.

variants.name: Disallow-to-live mapping
variants.payload: Take each Disallow path (e.g. /admin, /private/, /api/internal) and confirm it resolves to a real route.
variants.expect: A live, previously-hidden route is the lead; a 404 is not.
variants.why: robots.txt is an inventory hint; a hidden path is only material once the path actually exists.

variants.name: Wildcard and ordering
variants.payload:
GET /robots.txt HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Connection: close
variants.expect: Record Allow/Disallow ordering, wildcards, and Crawl-delay to interpret which paths are truly off-limits.
variants.why: Parser semantics decide whether a Disallow rule actually blocks a path, so the raw file must be read literally.

checks.title: sitemap.xml review
checks.why: A sitemap lists routes that may not be linked anywhere, exposing staging, parameterised, or post-login pages.
checks.validate: Cross-reference sitemap URLs against the route inventory; a sitemap entry alone is not a finding.

variants.name: Fetch sitemap.xml
variants.payload:
GET /sitemap.xml HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Connection: close
variants.expect: Enumerate <loc> URLs and <sitemap> indexes for sibling maps.
variants.why: A sitemap is the publisher’s own route list — a low-noise way to expand the inventory.

variants.name: Sitemap index chain
variants.payload:
GET /sitemap-index.xml HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Connection: close
variants.expect: Follow <sitemap> child entries and image/video extensions for more URLs.
variants.why: Indexed sites split sitemaps; the child files often hold the deeper or less-linked routes.

variants.name: Unlinked / parameterised URLs
variants.payload: Collect URLs with query strings, numeric IDs, or unusual extensions that do not appear in navigation.
variants.expect: Treat as route leads; confirm each before reporting.
variants.why: Sitemap-only URLs are exactly the routes a scanner walking navigation will miss.

checks.title: .well-known resources
checks.why: Standardized /.well-known/ endpoints publish security, identity, and capability metadata worth reviewing for leaks or mismatches.
checks.validate: A well-known resource is only a finding if it exposes sensitive material or mismatches the advertised security policy.

variants.name: security.txt
variants.payload:
GET /.well-known/security.txt HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Connection: close
variants.expect: Policy, contact, and disclosure endpoints. A missing file is informational; an outdated one is a process gap.
variants.why: security.txt is the canonical security-contact endpoint a responsible-disclosure reader checks first.

variants.name: Standard endpoint sweep
variants.payload:
/.well-known/openid-configuration
/.well-known/jwks.json
/.well-known/change-password
/.well-known/assetlinks.json
/.well-known/security.txt
variants.expect: Review each for leaked issuer config, JWKS key material, or mismatched redirect endpoints.
variants.why: The well-known namespace is a fixed, guessable contract, so a systematic sweep finds everything in one pass.

variants.name: applinks / assetlinks
variants.payload:
GET /.well-known/assetlinks.json HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Connection: close
variants.expect: App/domain association: verify a link you control cannot claim this domain’s deep links.
variants.why: Misconfigured association files can hand off deep-link authority to an attacker’s app.

checks.title: DNS records review
checks.why: Authoritative DNS exposes the host inventory, external services, and mail/SPF/DKIM posture before you touch the app.
checks.validate: Record a DNS finding only when it materially expands the attack surface or enables abuse (takeover, mail spoofing, sensitive host).

variants.name: A / AAAA / CNAME inventory
variants.payload:
dig +short A www.example.com
dig +short AAAA www.example.com
dig CNAME www.example.com
variants.expect: Map every hostname and CNAME target; each external CNAME is a potential takeover or dependency.
variants.why: CNAME chains reveal which assets are served by third parties — the highest-value recon output.

variants.name: MX / TXT / SPF / DMARC
variants.payload:
dig MX example.com
dig TXT example.com
dig TXT _dmarc.example.com
variants.expect: Mail routing and spoofing posture: missing SPF/DMARC or an open relay MX is the lead.
variants.why: Email-related records decide whether the domain can be spoofed, which is often an overlooked angle.

checks.title: Certificate transparency hostnames
checks.why: Certificate transparency logs reveal subdomains and staging hosts that never appear in DNS walking or search engines.
checks.validate: A CT-discovered host is a lead, not a finding; confirm each candidate resolves and is live before reporting.

variants.name: crt.sh search
variants.payload: curl -s 'https://crt.sh/?q=%25.example.com&output=json' | jq -r '.[].name_value' | sort -u
variants.expect: Collect every certificate-name candidate; dedupe and filter wildcards.
variants.why: CT logs index every cert ever issued, so they surface hosts DNS enumeration misses.

variants.name: Dedupe and resolve
variants.payload: for h in $(candidate-list); do dig +short "$h"; done | sort -u
variants.expect: Resolve each candidate to confirm it exists and points where you expect.
variants.why: A stale or non-resolving CT entry is noise; resolution is what turns it into a target.

checks.title: Dangling DNS / subdomain takeover
checks.why: A CNAME pointing at a decommissioned or unclaimed third-party service lets someone else control the subdomain.
checks.validate: Identification only — confirm the resource is dangling and claimable, but never claim or provision the third-party resource.

variants.name: Identify the dangling CNAME
variants.payload: dig CNAME legacy.example.com
variants.expect: A CNAME to a decommissioned SaaS (e.g. *.herokudns.com, *.azurewebsites.net) or an unclaimed bucket is the lead.
variants.why: Dangling CNAMEs are the classic takeover primitive; the first step is naming the target resource.

variants.name: Confirm unclaimed, do not claim
variants.payload: Check the provider’s takeover signature for that exact resource name. Do NOT create or take over the resource.
variants.expect: Report the dangling record and the provider it would claim; stop there.
variants.why: Authorized testing identifies the risk; claiming the resource crosses into affecting third-party infrastructure.

checks.title: Path / URL normalization
checks.why: Encoded slashes, duplicate slashes, semicolon matrix params, and dot-segment collapse can be normalized differently by the edge and the origin.
checks.validate: A normalization differential is a finding when it lets a request reach a path the edge intended to block (or lets traversal slip through).

variants.name: Encoded slash
variants.payload:
GET /%2fadmin HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Connection: close
variants.expect: Compare with /admin. If %2f reaches a route /admin blocks, routing differs between hops.
variants.why: An encoded slash decodes differently in the path parser than in routing, exposing the classic differential.

variants.name: Duplicate slashes
variants.payload:
GET //admin// HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Connection: close
variants.expect: Compare with /admin. If the app strips or keeps slashes differently than the edge, an allowlist can be bypassed.
variants.why: Duplicate and leading slashes are collapsed inconsistently, which breaks prefix allowlists.

variants.name: Semicolon / matrix params
variants.payload:
GET /admin;.css HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Connection: close
variants.expect: Spring and JAX-RS treat ; as a matrix-parameter separator; other stacks do not. Compare across endpoints.
variants.why: Matrix parameters change how a path is interpreted, so a suffix that should not match can.

variants.name: Dot-segment collapse
variants.payload:
GET /assets/./../admin HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Connection: close
variants.expect: Normalised to /admin at some hops and kept literal at others; use with a canary file for traversal checks.
variants.why: Dot-segments are collapsed by URL parsers, which is how traversal and allowlist bypasses appear.

groups.title: Client and cache
groups.summary: Published JS, CORS on static assets, and cache-key confusion through a CDN.

checks.title: Published JavaScript and source maps
checks.why: Bundles leak endpoints, feature flags, and occasionally real secrets. Maps reconstruct original source.
checks.validate: A live secret, internal URL, or non-public source tree is retrieved from a client-delivered asset.

variants.name: Grep first-party JS
variants.payload: api[_-]?key|secret|password|token|AKIA[0-9A-Z]{16}|sk_live_|ghp_|xox[baprs]-|Bearer [A-Za-z0-9._-]+
variants.expect: Confirm any hit is a live credential, not a public site key or a placeholder.
variants.why: Secret patterns in the bundle are the first-pass disclosure check.

variants.name: Source map
variants.payload:
GET /assets/app.js.map HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Connection: close
variants.expect: A JSON source map with sourcesContent. Readable client code is not a finding; embedded secrets or internal URLs are.
variants.why: A source map reconstructs original source.

variants.name: sourceMappingURL comment
variants.payload: //# sourceMappingURL=app.js.map
variants.expect: Follow every sourceMappingURL in published JS, including absolute CDN URLs.
variants.why: The trailing comment names the map even when it is not linked.

checks.title: CORS on the published origin
checks.why: A reflected ACAO on JSON or authenticated-looking responses lets another origin read them. Public HTML usually does not matter.
checks.validate: A controlled origin can read a non-public body. Wildcard ACAO on a brochure is not a finding.

variants.name: Reflected Origin
variants.payload:
GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Origin: https://evil.example
Connection: close
variants.expect: Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://evil.example is only a finding if the body is sensitive and credentials work.
variants.why: A reflected ACAO on a non-public response lets another origin read it.

variants.name: null origin
variants.payload:
GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Origin: null
Connection: close
variants.expect: ACAO: null is rarely justified on a public site. Still needs a readable sensitive body to report.
variants.why: A null Origin bypasses substring and allowlist regex checks.

checks.title: Cache key vs Host / unkeyed headers
checks.why: A CDN that keys on URL but not Host, or that caches a reflected header, will serve the poisoned page to other users.
checks.validate: A clean request for the canonical host receives the marker you injected on a different Host or unkeyed header. Use an isolated cache buster.

variants.name: Unkeyed X-Forwarded-Host into cache
variants.payload:
GET /?wapt=1 HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
X-Forwarded-Host: evil.example
Connection: close
variants.expect: If the body or a redirect reflects evil.example, immediately replay GET /?wapt=1 with a clean Host and no extra headers.
variants.why: A cache that keys on URL but not on an unkeyed header serves the poisoned page to other users.

variants.name: Unkeyed X-Forwarded-Scheme
variants.payload:
GET /?wapt=2 HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
X-Forwarded-Scheme: nothttps
Connection: close
variants.expect: Reflected into asset URLs or CSP? Replay clean. Purge the test key if it sticks.
variants.why: An unkeyed scheme header poisons the cached protocol.

variants.name: Cache deception via path suffix
variants.payload:
GET /index.html/wapt.css HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Connection: close
variants.expect: On a static site this is usually a 404. Still check if the CDN caches an HTML 200 under a .css key.
variants.why: A path suffix that maps to a dynamic page but caches as a static asset is cache deception.

checks.title: DOM XSS
checks.why: hash, search, or a path segment is written into innerHTML, eval, or a javascript: URL.
checks.validate: A marker in the URL executes in the real page. A sink in a bundle that is never reached is not a finding.

variants.name: Hash to HTML
variants.payload: https://www.example.com/# https://www.example.com/?q=
variants.expect: Grep the bundle for location.hash, location.search, document.write, innerHTML, insertAdjacentHTML.
variants.why: A hash fragment written into innerHTML is a DOM-XSS sink.

variants.name: javascript: navigation
variants.payload:
https://www.example.com/#javascript:alert(1)
https://www.example.com/?next=javascript:alert(1)
variants.expect: Must not become location.href / window.open. data:text/html is the same class.
variants.why: A javascript: URL assigned to location executes in the page.

checks.title: DOM open redirect
checks.why: Client-side navigation (location, router, window.open) accepts an absolute or javascript: URL.
checks.validate: The page navigates off-origin or into a javascript: URL. A reflected string that is not used as a URL is not enough.

variants.name: Absolute next
variants.payload:
https://www.example.com/?next=https://evil.example/
https://www.example.com/?next=//evil.example/
variants.expect: Watch location.assign / href / replace / router.push after load.
variants.why: A client-side navigation accepting an absolute URL is an open redirect.

variants.name: javascript: next
variants.payload: https://www.example.com/?next=javascript:alert(1)
variants.expect: Must be rejected. This is XSS, not just a redirect.
variants.why: A javascript: next URL is a DOM-XSS sink.

checks.title: Client-side secrets
checks.why: The published bundle contains a live privileged secret, not a public site key.
checks.validate: A retrieved value authenticates as a privileged identity or signs a privileged request. A public Stripe pk_ or Mapbox token is not a finding.

variants.name: Grep the bundle
variants.payload: api[_-]?key|secret|password|token|AKIA[0-9A-Z]{16}|sk_live_|ghp_|xox[baprs]-|Bearer [A-Za-z0-9._-]+
variants.expect: Confirm any hit is a live credential.
variants.why: Secret patterns in the published bundle are the first-pass disclosure check.

variants.name: Inline and comments
variants.payload: View-source: <script> blocks, data- attributes, HTML comments.
variants.expect: Same validation as the bundle. Redact in evidence.
variants.why: Secrets hidden in inline scripts and comments are easy to miss.

checks.title: Prototype pollution
checks.why: Query, hash, or JSON is merged into an object without blocking __proto__ / constructor / prototype.
checks.validate: A gadget you control changes application behaviour (XSS sink, bypass, or privilege). A silent merge into Object.prototype without impact is a weakness, not yet a reportable finding.

variants.name: Query gadget
variants.payload:
https://www.example.com/?__proto__[polluted]=wapt
https://www.example.com/?constructor[prototype][polluted]=wapt
variants.expect: After load, Object.prototype.polluted === "wapt" in the console is the weakness. Then hunt a gadget.
variants.why: A __proto__/constructor key in the query reaches a merge into an object.

variants.name: JSON merge
variants.payload: {"__proto__": {"polluted": "wapt"}}
variants.expect: Any JSON.parse + recursive merge of user JSON (config, postMessage, storage) is in scope.
variants.why: A JSON merge can pollute the prototype when the parser handles __proto__ literally.

checks.title: postMessage security
checks.why: The page listens for message and trusts event.data without checking event.origin.
checks.validate: A page you control can drive a sink or an authenticated action. A listener that ignores unknown origins is not a finding.

variants.name: Listener inventory
variants.payload:
addEventListener('message', …)
onmessage = …
variants.expect: For each listener, record whether origin is compared to an exact allowlist (===, not indexOf).
observe: data used as HTML / nav / token
variants.why: Enumerating listeners shows which handlers trust event.data.

variants.name: Drive from an opener
variants.payload:
<script>const w = window.open('https://www.example.com/');
setTimeout(() => w.postMessage({type:'setToken', token:'wapt'}, '*'), 1500);</script>
variants.expect: Must be ignored. A token or HTML sink accepting this is the finding. Use a test account.
variants.why: A controlled window sends a message to confirm an origin-unchecked handler.

checks.title: Third-party JavaScript
checks.why: Analytics, widgets, and tag managers run with the origin's privileges.
checks.validate: A third-party script can read sensitive DOM or cookies, or a compromised supply-chain host would execute here. Presence of analytics is not a finding.

variants.name: Inventory
variants.payload: Document every script[src] host. Compare with CSP script-src.
variants.expect: Unexpected hosts, http:// scripts on https, or a tag manager that can inject arbitrary JS.
variants.why: Listing third-party scripts shows what runs with origin privileges.

variants.name: SRI and CSP
variants.payload:
GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Connection: close
variants.expect: integrity= on third-party scripts; CSP script-src pinning. Missing SRI on a static brochure is a lead.
observe: Whether a host can be swapped
variants.why: SRI and a constrained CSP bound what third-party scripts can do.

checks.title: Web Storage security
checks.why: Tokens and personal data in localStorage/sessionStorage are readable by any script on the origin and survive in the browser after logout.
checks.validate: A finding is when sensitive data — tokens, PII, or session material — is kept in browser storage instead of a short-lived HttpOnly cookie.

variants.name: Storage inventory
variants.payload: In DevTools run: Object.entries(localStorage).forEach(([k,v])=>console.log(k,v)); repeat for sessionStorage.
variants.expect: List every key; flag tokens, PII, and session identifiers.
variants.why: The inventory decides whether a leak is real: a cart id is noise, an access token is a finding.

variants.name: Logout persistence
variants.payload: Log out, then re-read localStorage and sessionStorage on the logged-out page.
variants.expect: Sensitive values that survive logout remain readable and reusable.
variants.why: Persisting across logout means a shared device keeps the token available to the next user.

checks.title: Service worker scope
checks.why: A service worker controls navigation and caching for its scope; a too-broad scope or a cached sensitive response can be abused or leak data.
checks.validate: A finding is when the worker scope covers more than its origin needs, or it caches authenticated/sensitive responses.

variants.name: Locate the worker
variants.payload:
GET /sw.js HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Connection: close
variants.expect: Find the registration script and its Scope from the SW registration (DevTools → Application → Service Workers).
variants.why: The script and scope decide what the worker intercepts, so both must be read first.

variants.name: Caching of sensitive responses
variants.payload: Inspect cache.addAll / caches.put calls and the worker’s fetch handler for /api, /account, or authenticated responses.
variants.expect: Caching authenticated or account-specific responses in the Cache API is the lead.
variants.why: A worker that caches auth responses can serve one user’s data to the next on a shared browser.

checks.title: CSP nonces unpredictable without unsafe fallbacks
checks.why: A predictable nonce (counter, timestamp, short random) makes strict CSP equivalent to unsafe-inline.
checks.validate: Nonces are >= 128-bit random per response, never reused across responses, and no unsafe-inline fallback coexists.

variants.name: Nonce entropy sample
variants.payload: Collect 20+ responses; extract nonce values; check length, charset, repetition, and shared values across users/sessions.
variants.expect: 16+ base64 chars, no repetition, no cross-session reuse; any pattern is a finding.
variants.why: Your own responses are the whole sample.

variants.name: Nonce replay
variants.payload: Replay a captured nonce-bearing response nonce in a crafted script tag against a fresh page load (own test page).
variants.expect: Old nonce rejected — strictly per-response.
variants.why: Per-response means per-response.

variants.name: Fallback hunt
variants.payload: Check the policy for unsafe-inline alongside nonces, and script-src duplicate directives.
variants.expect: No unsafe-inline coexistence; duplicate script-src understood (second ignored per spec — a misconfig trap).
variants.why: The fallback quietly deletes the protection.

checks.title: CSP constrains base, object, and navigation
checks.why: Without base-uri/object-src/form-action restrictions, injected markup can hijack relative URLs, load plugins, or exfiltrate via form posts.
checks.validate: base-uri restricted (self or none), object-src none, form-action/frame-ancestors/navigation constrained where applicable.

variants.name: Base injection
variants.payload: On your test page or an HTML injection point, inject <base href="https://evil.example/"> and observe resource loads.
variants.expect: base-uri restricts or none blocks hijack of relative script/style URLs.
variants.why: base-uri is the forgotten CSP directive with the biggest payoff.

variants.name: Object/plugin probe
variants.payload: Attempt <object data="https://evil.example/x.swf"> style embeds at any injection point.
variants.expect: object-src none blocks plugin-style loads.
variants.why: Legacy vectors still ship in modern apps.

variants.name: Form-action exfil
variants.payload: Inject a form posting credentials to your Collaborator domain; submit it yourself.
variants.expect: form-action blocks the cross-origin post (or is documented as open).
variants.why: Exfiltration does not need script.

checks.title: X-Frame-Options consistent with frame-ancestors
checks.why: Conflicting legacy and modern framing headers leave clickjacking protection to browser quirks.
checks.validate: Where both exist, XFO and CSP frame-ancestors agree; where only legacy exists, it is deliberately documented.

variants.name: Header pair audit
variants.payload: curl -sI https://www.example.com | grep -iE "x-frame-options|frame-ancestors" across main, auth, and error routes.
variants.expect: Values agree (DENY/none, SAMEORIGIN/self) on every route; conflicts listed.
variants.why: The audit is one command per route.

variants.name: Frame probe
variants.payload: Embed the app in an iframe on your test origin; observe behavior.
variants.expect: Blocked consistently; no route that renders in a foreign frame.
variants.why: Behavior beats headers.

variants.name: Legacy-only note
variants.payload: Where only XFO survives, record the decision (legacy browser policy) for the report.
variants.expect: Documented reason; modern frame-ancestors preferred.
variants.why: Legacy headers need funerals too.

checks.title: Accurate Content-Type and charset everywhere
checks.why: Wrong or missing content-types let browsers sniff active content — the road to stored XSS via uploads and API responses rendered as HTML.
checks.validate: Every response carries an accurate Content-Type with charset; user-content endpoints never default to text/html.

variants.name: Route-type census
variants.payload: curl -sI across HTML, JSON, JS, CSS, downloads, SVG, and error routes; tabulate Content-Type + charset.
variants.expect: Accurate type and charset on every route; JSON never text/html; SVG image/svg+xml (with CSP thought through).
variants.why: One census, permanent reference table.

variants.name: Sniff probe
variants.payload: Fetch a JSON/upload endpoint containing HTML-ish canary content with an Accept: text/html and via direct navigation.
variants.expect: No sniff-to-HTML execution; X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff present on non-HTML.
variants.why: nosniff plus correct types is the pair that works.

variants.name: Upload-type honesty
variants.payload: Re-check Content-Type on the download URL of an uploaded file you control.
variants.expect: Served type matches the safe delivery policy (see file-handling checks).
variants.why: The header is the last word on parsing.

checks.title: COOP where cross-window isolation matters
checks.why: Without COOP, opened windows keep references (and some leak channels) into your app — tabnabbing and XS-leak plumbing.
checks.validate: Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy set (same-origin) on pages with authenticated state, aligned with popup/window usage.

variants.name: Opener reference probe
variants.payload: From your test page, window.open the app and inspect the opener relationship both ways in console.
variants.expect: References severed per COOP; document actual isolation.
variants.why: The direct behavioral test.

variants.name: Tabnabbing combo
variants.payload: Open an external link (marked rel=noopener?) from the app; from the external side attempt opener.location changes (your own pages).
variants.expect: rel=noopener and/or COOP prevent reverse tabnabbing.
variants.why: Pairs with the client-side tabnabbing check.

variants.name: Isolation-inventory note
variants.payload: Inventory which authenticated routes set COOP and which legitimately need cross-window access.
variants.expect: COOP on authenticated surfaces unless a documented feature needs otherwise.
variants.why: Isolation is a per-route decision set.

checks.title: COEP only where isolation requires it
checks.why: COEP enables cross-origin isolation (SharedArrayBuffer, precise timers) — attackers want it too; deploy deliberately, not by cargo cult.
checks.validate: COEP/CORP appear only on surfaces needing isolation; embedded resources carry CORP/credentials policy consistently.

variants.name: Isolation census
variants.payload: Check COEP/CORP/COOP across routes; identify which features demand isolation (SAB, precise timers).
variants.expect: Isolation present exactly where needed; no accidental blanket COEP breaking legit embeds.
variants.why: Map intent before judging.

variants.name: Embed breakage probe
variants.payload: Embed legit third-party resources (analytics, fonts, images) on COEP pages.
variants.expect: Intended resources load (CORP/cors-approved) — breakage shows accidental policy.
variants.why: Broken embeds reveal unmanaged policy.

variants.name: SAB abuse surface note
variants.payload: Where isolation exists, note which high-resolution side channels it unlocks for the threat model.
variants.expect: Documented in report as deliberate trade-off.
variants.why: Isolation is also an attacker capability.

checks.title: Clear-Site-Data on high-risk logout/reset
checks.why: Shared machines keep tokens and caches after logout unless the server explicitly clears client state.
checks.validate: High-risk logout (and credential reset) responses carry Clear-Site-Data scoped to what the app uses, alongside server-side revocation.

variants.name: Logout residue sweep
variants.payload: Inventory storage + caches before/after logout (DevTools Application).
variants.expect: Tokens, caches, and storage cleared (header or script) — nothing revivable locally.
variants.why: The before/after diff is the evidence.

variants.name: Header scope check
variants.payload: Inspect the Clear-Site-Data directive values on logout responses.
variants.expect: Scoped to "cache","storage" (or documented subset); wildcards only if everything is client-clearable.
variants.why: The header is a scalpel, not a fog.

variants.name: Reset-flow parity
variants.payload: Password reset / device revocation flows: same clearing behavior.
variants.expect: Credential events clear client state like logout does.
variants.why: Resets are compromise responses.

checks.title: Safe Content-Disposition on downloads
checks.why: Downloaded files with attacker-influenced names and inline dispositions execute in the origin context or deceive users.
checks.validate: Downloads carry attachment; filename encoded and sanitized; no inline active content from user data.

variants.name: Filename injection
variants.payload: Upload/download a file named with quotes, CR/LF, Unicode lookalikes, and .html double extensions (your own file).
variants.expect: Header stays well-formed; dangerous names neutralized; no header splitting.
variants.why: Response-splitting via filenames is the classic.

variants.name: Inline disposition probe
variants.payload: Fetch the download URL directly in the browser.
variants.expect: attachment (or a hardened inline policy for previews) — user content never renders as origin HTML.
variants.why: inline + text/html = stored XSS via upload.

variants.name: Charset on downloads
variants.payload: Check Content-Type + charset pairs on CSV/TSV exports.
variants.expect: Safe types (text/csv) with neutral charset; no Excel formula injection left to the client (see file-handling depth).
variants.why: Exports are user data too.

checks.title: Product and version headers minimized
checks.why: Server/X-Powered-By and framework versions hand attackers a targeted exploit shortlist for free.
checks.validate: Version-bearing headers removed or generic; disclosure limited to what operations require.

variants.name: Header census
variants.payload: curl -sI on main/API/error routes; list Server, X-Powered-By, and friends.
variants.expect: Removed or generic; anything kept has an operational reason.
variants.why: Free reconnaissance, countered for free.

variants.name: Error-page versions
variants.payload: Trigger 404/500 pages; grep bodies for version strings, framework signatures, build ids.
variants.expect: Error bodies version-free.
variants.why: Bodies leak more than headers.

variants.name: Asset metadata note
variants.payload: Check meta generators, build-id headers, and sourcemap references for version leakage.
variants.expect: Build identifiers absent in production or documented.
variants.why: Build ids fingerprint exact deployments.

checks.title: Obsolete X-XSS-Protection disabled
checks.why: The legacy auditor is dead and was itself exploitable — its presence signals stale security practice.
checks.validate: X-XSS-Protection absent or explicitly 0; no reliance on it anywhere.

variants.name: Header check
variants.payload: curl -sI | grep -i x-xss-protection across routes.
variants.expect: Absent or "0" — never "1" modes.
variants.why: One command.

variants.name: Mode audit
variants.payload: If present, note mode=block vs report URLs.
variants.expect: No report= URLs (they leaked cross-origin); recommend removal.
variants.why: Even the correct spelling is obsolete.

checks.title: HPKP not deployed
checks.why: Public key pinning is deprecated and historically brick devices and enables ransom-style lockout — its presence is a risk, not a control.
checks.validate: No Public-Key-Pins headers on any route; certificate assurance handled via modern mechanisms.

variants.name: Pin hunt
variants.payload: curl -sI across routes grepping Public-Key-Pins and Public-Key-Pins-Report-Only.
variants.expect: Absent everywhere.
variants.why: The check is the finding.

variants.name: Ops-inventory note
variants.payload: Where pins existed historically, confirm removal ran its max-age course and monitoring is off.
variants.expect: No stale pin trust anywhere including subdomains.
variants.why: Pins outlive the teams that set them.

checks.title: Expect-CT treated as obsolete telemetry
checks.why: Expect-CT is deprecated; keeping it implies a CT story that no longer works that way.
checks.validate: Expect-CT absent; certificate transparency handled by current monitoring.

variants.name: Header check
variants.payload: grep for Expect-CT across routes.
variants.expect: Absent; if present, removal recommended with the CT monitoring story confirmed.
variants.why: Header census covers it.

variants.name: CT monitoring note
variants.payload: Ask/verify how CT logs are monitored today (issuer monitoring, domain watches).
variants.expect: A current mechanism exists and is owned.
variants.why: Replace, do not just remove.

checks.title: Policies consistent across routes, errors, redirects
checks.why: Security headers vanish on error pages, redirects, and alternate origins — attackers route to the weakest copy of the app.
checks.validate: The full header set applies to every route, status code, redirect hop, and alternate origin (www vs apex, API vs web).

variants.name: Status-code matrix
variants.payload: Request normal, 401, 403, 404, 500, and redirect routes; diff header sets.
variants.expect: Identical policy headers on every status; gaps listed as findings.
variants.why: Error handlers forget headers first.

variants.name: Origin matrix
variants.payload: Repeat across www/apex, api subdomain, and staged alternate hosts.
variants.expect: Policy consistent across origins in scope.
variants.why: The weakest origin is the attack surface.

variants.name: Redirect-hop follow
variants.payload: Follow each redirect chain with curl -L -I; check each hop.
variants.expect: Every hop carries the policy (HSTS on the first, CSP on the rendering hop).
variants.why: Hops skip middleware sometimes.

checks.title: Duplicate and malformed headers rejected consistently
checks.why: Duplicate CSP/HSTS headers and odd casing let intermediaries and browsers pick the weakest interpretation.
checks.validate: Duplicate security headers are rejected or normalized; the server never emits two policies for one directive.

variants.name: Duplicate request-header probe
variants.payload: Send requests with duplicated Origin, Host variants, and repeated cookie names; observe normalization.
variants.expect: Deterministic handling; no 500s, no policy bypass via duplicates.
variants.why: Request duplicates test middleware maturity.

variants.name: Response self-audit
variants.payload: Check responses for accidentally duplicated headers (middleware stacking).
variants.expect: Single, consistent values — duplicates reported.
variants.why: Stacks emit what stacks emit.

variants.name: Case/whitespace roulette
variants.payload: Request headers with odd casing, tabs, and folded values.
variants.expect: Parsed consistently; parser differentials documented.
variants.why: Intermediaries normalize differently than origins.

checks.title: Report-only distinguished from enforcement
checks.why: A Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only that everyone believes is enforcement is a false sense of security worth naming.
checks.validate: Report-Only usage is deliberate, monitored, and time-boxed; enforced policies exist where protection is claimed.

variants.name: Policy census
variants.payload: List which routes send Report-Only vs enforced variants.
variants.expect: Report-Only only on documented rollout paths; enforced elsewhere.
variants.why: The census names the gap.

variants.name: Report endpoint check
variants.payload: Where report URIs exist, confirm the endpoint receives and owns reports.
variants.expect: Reports flow to a monitored endpoint; failures visible.
variants.why: Report endpoints leak URLs — protect them.

variants.name: Rollout-window note
variants.payload: Check how long Report-Only has been the state (changelog/headers history if available).
variants.expect: Time-boxed rollouts; permanent Report-Only flagged.
variants.why: Temporary things become permanent.

arbitrary-host.purpose: The most basic probe: does the origin trust an attacker-chosen Host for routing, generated URLs, or cache keys?
arbitrary-host.payload:
GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: evil.example
Connection: close

duplicate-host.purpose: Tests front-end/back-end disagreement in Host parsing.
duplicate-host.payload:
GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Host: evil.example
Connection: close

duplicate-host-reversed.purpose: Order sensitivity: some stacks take the first Host, others the last.
duplicate-host-reversed.payload:
GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: evil.example
Host: www.example.com
Connection: close

host-normalization.purpose: Case, trailing dot, and default port must not change routing or generated URLs.
host-normalization.payload:
GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: EXAMPLE.COM
Connection: close

host-with-port.purpose: A port-suffixed Host must resolve to the same authority, not a parse trick.
host-with-port.payload:
GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com:443
Connection: close

absolute-form-target.purpose: Absolute-form request-target lets a request carry a second authority alongside Host.
absolute-form-target.payload:
GET https://evil.example/ HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Connection: close

x-forwarded-host.purpose: Tests whether a trusted proxy header overrides the externally controlled authority.
x-forwarded-host.payload:
GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
X-Forwarded-Host: evil.example
Connection: close

x-host-forwarded-server.purpose: Java/IIS stacks sometimes prefer these over X-Forwarded-Host.
x-host-forwarded-server.payload:
GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
X-Host: evil.example
X-Forwarded-Server: evil.example
Connection: close

forwarded-rfc7239.purpose: The standardised Forwarded header must only be trusted from an authenticated hop.
forwarded-rfc7239.payload:
GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Forwarded: host=evil.example;proto=https
Connection: close

x-forwarded-proto-downgrade.purpose: A downgrade to http:// must not flip cookies or redirects to plaintext.
x-forwarded-proto-downgrade.payload:
GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
X-Forwarded-Proto: http
X-Forwarded-Scheme: http
Connection: close

line-wrapped-host.purpose: Suffix and look-alike hosts probe substring allowlist bypasses.
line-wrapped-host.payload:
GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Host: www.example.com.evil.example
Connection: close
